name: Pancragen
summary: A four-amino-acid peptide (Lys-Glu-Asp-Trp) from Russian 'bioregulator' research, promoted for pancreas function and blood sugar; tested in cells, monkeys and small human studies.
what_it_is: Pancragen is a lab-made chain of four amino acids: lysine, glutamic acid, aspartic acid and tryptophan (Lys-Glu-Asp-Trp, or KEDW). The US National Library of Medicine indexes it under that name; it comes from Vladimir Khavinson's peptide research in Russia, where it is listed as a dietary supplement. In cell studies it switched on genes that pancreatic cells need to mature and make hormones, and its developers patented it to lower blood sugar in diabetes.

evidence.why: Cell, rat and monkey studies plus two small human studies in diabetes, one in a journal and one in a patent, all involving the developer's group.

status_us.label: Not FDA-approved; not on FDA compounding lists
status_us.note: Pancragen is not an FDA-approved drug and appears on none of FDA's compounding lists (nominated substances, updated May 2026; safety-risk and withdrawn nominations, April 2026). FDA allows pharmacy compounding only from ingredients that are in an approved drug, meet a USP standard, or are on or under review for its bulk list; Russia's drug register lists it as a dietary supplement.

benefits.claim: Lower fasting blood sugar, insulin and insulin resistance in a small study of older adults with type 2 diabetes
More people could lower their insulin dose, and fewer needed to raise it, in a small study of 36 people with diabetes described in the developer's patent
Faster clearing of sugar from the blood and normal insulin responses in old rhesus monkeys
Lower blood sugar, more insulin and better survival in rats with chemically induced diabetes
Restored markers of mature pancreatic cells in aging cell cultures

risks.risk: Low blood sugar is possible if combined with insulin or other diabetes medicines, given its reported glucose-lowering effect
Human safety has only been reported by the developers; the patent calls it non-toxic without describing the tests
No FDA-approved or pharmacy-compounded version exists, so products may not match the peptide that was studied

avoid_if: Diabetes treated with insulin or other glucose-lowering medicines, unless your clinician is involved
Pancreatitis or other pancreas disease, unless a clinician is involved
interactions: Insulin and other glucose-lowering medicines: possible added blood-sugar lowering (not formally studied)

during: Blood sugar checks if you take diabetes medicines
labs.why: No evidence-based monitoring exists for Pancragen; blood sugar is the sensible marker because that is what the studies measured.

studies.title: Prospects of Using Pancragen for Correction of Metabolic Disorders in Elderly People
studies.people: 63 older adults: 33 with type 2 diabetes and 30 healthy
studies.finding: In people with diabetes who took pancragen, fasting glucose, glucose tolerance, insulin and insulin resistance improved, while those who did not take it showed no change. The abstract does not describe randomization.

studies.title: Impact of tetrapeptide pancragen on endocrine function of the pancreas in old monkeys
studies.people: Old and young female rhesus monkeys
studies.finding: In old monkeys, pancragen sped up clearance of sugar after a glucose load and normalized insulin and C-peptide responses; part of the effect lasted three weeks after it was stopped.

studies.title: Effects of Pancragen on The Differentiation of Pancreatic Cells During Their Ageing
studies.people: Young and aged pancreatic cell cultures
studies.finding: Aged cultures lost markers of mature pancreatic cells; pancragen raised markers such as Pdx1 and Ptf1a back toward, or above, young levels.

ask_your_clinician: Could this cause low blood sugar with my current diabetes medicines?
Which blood sugar tests should I track, and how often?
Is there stronger evidence for other options to manage my blood sugar?

notes_for_editor: The best-documented of the Khavinson bioregulators in this batch, but every study involves the developer (Khavinson) as an author or patent holder. Korkushko 2011 (63 older adults) does not describe randomization, dosing or duration in the abstract; the patent's 36-patient study reports inconsistent group sizes and is not peer reviewed. The monkey study (PMID 25946840, in Russian) was read via a university library catalog record because PubMed would not load; animal numbers were not given. The 2013 cell study describes its cells as MIA PaCa-2 embryonic acinar cultures; worth checking that cell line's origin. Russian supplement status was seen on the RLS register's group listing only.
